title: Design a Digital Wallet System (like Paytm/Google Pay) — balance management with double-entry bookkeeping, idempotent top-up/payment/refund operations, optimistic locking or conditional updates for balance, transaction ledger (append-only audit trail), P2P transfers (debit sender + credit receiver atomically), integration with payment gateways, fraud detection, daily/monthly transaction limits, settlement and reconciliation, and handling partial failures.
shortTitle: Design a Digital Wallet System (like Paytm/Google Pay)

s1_definition.profdef: A digital wallet system maintains user balances backed by a double-entry append-only ledger, supports idempotent top-up, payment, refund, and peer-to-peer transfer operations, protects balances with optimistic locking or conditional updates to prevent lost updates, integrates with external payment gateways for bank funding, enforces daily and monthly limits, runs fraud detection, and reconciles its ledger against gateway records while handling partial failures gracefully.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh keeps money in his National Bank of India wallet app. He tops it up from his bank, pays Priya for groceries, and sometimes gets a refund. Every rupee movement is written twice in the wallet's books — out of one place, into another — so the totals always balance. If his phone sends the same payment twice because of a network glitch, the wallet recognizes it and charges him once. The wallet also stops him exceeding a daily spend limit, flags suspicious bursts, and at day's end checks its own books against the bank's records to make sure nothing is missing.
s1_definition.oneliner: Back every wallet balance with an idempotent, double-entry, append-only ledger, protect updates with optimistic locking, enforce limits, detect fraud, and reconcile against the gateway.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A digital wallet system maintains user balances backed by a double-entry append-only ledger, supports idempotent top-up, payment, refund, and peer-to-peer transfer operations, protects balances with optimistic locking or conditional updates to prevent lost updates, integrates with external payment gateways for bank funding, enforces daily and monthly limits, runs fraud detection, and reconciles its ledger against gateway records while handling partial failures gracefully.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Rajesh keeps money in his National Bank of India wallet app. He tops it up from his bank, pays Priya for groceries, and sometimes gets a refund. Every rupee movement is written twice in the wallet's books — out of one place, into another — so the totals always balance. If his phone sends the same payment twice because of a network glitch, the wallet recognizes it and charges him once. The wallet also stops him exceeding a daily spend limit, flags suspicious bursts, and at day's end checks its own books against the bank's records to make sure nothing is missing.

**One line to remember:** Back every wallet balance with an idempotent, double-entry, append-only ledger, protect updates with optimistic locking, enforce limits, detect fraud, and reconcile against the gateway.

sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — Rajesh tops up his wallet from his bank, and the top-up request is retried after a timeout. Without protection he would be charged twice. The real problem is safe retries. This is exactly how idempotency keys work.

Problem 2 — Rajesh and Priya both try operations on shared or rapidly changing balances, and two concurrent debits could each read the old balance and both succeed, overspending. The real problem is the lost-update race. This is exactly how optimistic locking with a version column prevents it.

Problem 3 — a peer-to-peer transfer must move money out of Rajesh and into Priya as one indivisible act, the books must always balance, and the bank must stop Rajesh exceeding his daily limit. These are exactly the atomic double-entry transfer and limit-enforcement features.

We build a runnable wallet core: a `WalletRepository` with versioned balances, a `Ledger` of append-only double entries, an `IdempotencyStore`, a `LimitService`, and a `WalletService` supporting top-up, transfer, and refund. The demo tops up Rajesh, retries the top-up to prove idempotency, transfers to Priya atomically, hits a daily limit, and prints the balanced ledger.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is a fifteen thousand rupee top-up for Rajesh (retried once), a five thousand transfer to Priya, and an over-limit eighteen thousand transfer, with a daily limit of twenty thousand.

Step 1: The first top-up sees a new idempotency key, posts a double entry debiting the funding bank and crediting Rajesh's wallet, and credits his balance to fifteen thousand. The key is recorded.

Step 2: The retried top-up with the same key finds it already seen and returns immediately, so Rajesh is not credited twice. His balance stays fifteen thousand.

Step 3: The transfer to Priya checks the daily limit, adding five thousand to today's spend, which is under twenty thousand. It reads Rajesh's version, does a conditional debit that succeeds because the version matches and funds suffice, credits Priya, and posts a transfer double entry. Rajesh drops to ten thousand and Priya rises to ten thousand.

Step 4: The eighteen thousand transfer checks the limit: five already spent plus eighteen is twenty-three thousand, over the twenty thousand cap, so the limit service throws and the transfer is blocked before any money moves. The ledger, containing only completed operations, still sums to zero.

```
2026-10-31 23:30:00 [INFO] Topped up WAL-RAJESH Rs.15000
2026-10-31 23:30:00 [WARNING] Idempotent top-up idem-topup-1
2026-10-31 23:30:00 [INFO] Rajesh balance: 15000
2026-10-31 23:30:00 [INFO] Transferred Rs.5000 WAL-RAJESH -> WAL-PRIYA
2026-10-31 23:30:00 [INFO] Rajesh=10000 Priya=10000
2026-10-31 23:30:00 [WARNING] Blocked: daily limit Rs.20000 exceeded for WAL-RAJESH
2026-10-31 23:30:00 [INFO] Ledger balances to zero: true
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  topUp(idem-topup-1, WAL-RAJESH, 15000)
    │
    ├─ FIRST (key new)                 ├─ RETRY (key seen)
    │  ledger.post(FUNDING→RAJESH)     │  return, no change
    │  credit RAJESH +15000            │
    ▼                                  ▼
  balance 15000                      balance 15000 (not doubled)

  transfer(idem-p2p-1, RAJESH→PRIYA, 5000)
    │ limits.checkAndAdd(5000) (under 20000)
    │ debit RAJESH (version match)
    │ credit PRIYA +5000
    │ ledger.post(TRANSFER debit+credit)
    ▼
  RAJESH 10000, PRIYA 10000

  transfer(idem-p2p-2, RAJESH→PRIYA, 18000)
    │ limits.checkAndAdd: 5000+18000=23000 > 20000
    ▼
  IllegalStateException (blocked, no money moved)

  Ledger: all entries sum to 0
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A digital wallet system maintains user balances backed by a double-entry, append-only ledger, and that ledger is the foundation of everything. Every operation produces two matching entries, so a top-up credits the user's wallet and debits a funding source, and a payment debits the payer and credits the payee. Because every debit has a matching credit, the signed sum of all entries is always zero and the books always balance, which gives me a tamper-evident audit trail that regulators require.

Two correctness mechanisms sit on top of the ledger. The first is idempotency: every top-up, payment, and transfer carries a client-generated key, and the server records the outcome under that key, so when Rajesh's phone retries a top-up after a timeout, it returns the same result rather than crediting him twice. The second is optimistic locking: each wallet row has a version, and a debit only succeeds if the version is unchanged since it was read, so two concurrent debits cannot both read the old balance and overspend. For peer-to-peer transfers I wrap the debit and credit in a single database transaction, so a crash can never debit one side without crediting the other.

Around this core I add limits, fraud detection, and reconciliation. Daily and monthly caps are checked before each spend, which both satisfies regulation and limits the damage from a compromised account, as the demo showed when an over-limit transfer was blocked before any money moved. Fraud detection scores transactions on velocity, amount, and device signals to block or challenge suspicious ones. Settlement and reconciliation run as scheduled jobs that move funds with partner banks and compare the wallet ledger against gateway statements.

The hardest real-world problem, and the one I always raise as a senior point, is partial failure. If a top-up succeeds at the external payment gateway but the local database write fails, the customer's money is in limbo, and silently losing it is unacceptable in banking. So the reconciliation job detects a gateway credit with no matching ledger entry and repairs it, crediting the wallet the customer is owed. Designing idempotency, optimistic locking, atomic transfers, and reconciliation together is what makes a wallet trustworthy enough to hold real people's money.
